Context documents reveal that Western Alaska fuel distribution adds approximately $1.00 per gallon in distribution costs plus $1.60 per gallon in local community costs to the network price. Distribution costs include: fuel lifting-fee at refinery (6¢), transport from refinery to regional hub (19¢), hub facility fee (3¢), transport from hub to community (60¢), and distributor's working capital/admin (10¢). Local costs include: tank farm capital (61¢), working capital (10¢), tank farm operations (83¢), and charges for other purposes (unknown). This means network routing costs represent only ~30% of real-world fuel delivery expenses.

Linehaul barges transporting fuel to regional hubs require 2.5-3.5 million gallon capacity shipments, making small deliveries to 1,000 gallon hub communities economically infeasible. Regional hubs include Dillingham, Naknek, Bethel, Nome, and Kotzebue. Small barges then deliver from hubs to communities, representing the most expensive distribution cost. Many communities have poor moorage and unloading equipment, adding to costs and risks. This economic reality explains why the network's 1,000 gallon hub capacities are operationally unsustainable for bulk fuel delivery.

Rural Alaska communities face extreme economic challenges: 1 in 5 Alaska school children from families receiving public assistance, rising to 6 in 10 in some rural areas. High rates of alcohol-related deaths and Fetal Alcohol Syndrome (4 times state rate, 10 times U.S. rate among Alaska Natives). Utility costs for remote communities increased from 6.6% to 9.9% of total income (2000-2006), compared to Anchorage's increase from 2.6% to 3.1%. These socio-economic factors create communities with limited ability to pay for fuel despite high needs.

The capacity-volume mismatch identified by the contrarian is validated by context documents: 19 of 20 hubs have 1,000 gallon capacity but linehaul barges require 2.5-3.5 million gallon shipments. This creates operational impossibility - deliveries would either overflow storage or be economically infeasible. The network routing represents mathematical optimization within impossible physical constraints, highlighting the disconnect between network data and real-world fuel logistics.

Future planning must address storage capacity as primary constraint before routing optimization. Recommendations: 1) Advocate for storage upgrades beyond 1,000 gallon capacities, 2) Develop Stebbins (817,800 gal) as true regional distribution hub with staging capabilities, 3) Implement delivery scheduling that matches actual storage volumes, 4) Consider tank farm replacement/repair programs given context documents show many tanks have fallen into disrepair due to lack of maintenance funds.

Integrate Power Cost Equalization (PCE) program considerations into fuel delivery planning. The PCE program subsidizes electricity costs in rural communities ($0.30/kWh residential, $0.25/kWh community facilities). Fuel deliveries for electricity generation should be coordinated with PCE cycles and community ability to pay. This represents a critical lifeline program that affects community viability and fuel demand patterns.

The contrarian's finding about remote facility limbo is exacerbated by context documents showing extreme last-mile challenges: remote facilities require specialized delivery beyond hub arrival, but communities have limited economic capacity to fund such deliveries. With utility costs already consuming 9.9% of income in remote communities (vs 3.1% in Anchorage), additional last-mile delivery costs could be economically devastating, creating an impossible choice between service and affordability.

Address seasonal coverage gaps with realistic transition strategies: Spring thaw (April-May) when barge access increases from 3% to 78-97% requires coordinated planning; Fall freeze-up (October-November) when barge access drops from 99% to 8% creates critical vulnerability windows. Develop month-by-month delivery strategies that account for actual passability patterns and community fuel needs throughout the annual cycle, not just peak summer and deep winter.

claims.text: The plan implements seasonal routing optimization: summer barge deliveries (August) for coastal hubs like Nome, Unalakleet, Shishmaref, Koyuk, and Stebbins when 99.8% of barge edges are passable, versus only 3% in winter months. Winter deliveries (January) use road/plane combinations for inland hubs like Fairbanks and Saint Michael when barge access is limited.

Cost-optimized multimodal routing uses barge ($0.001/gal-mile) for long coastal segments, road ($0.0007/gal-mile) for land access, and plane ($0.025/gal-mile) only when necessary, with transfer fees ($0.24/gal) at mode changes. The Nome-Teller-Brevig Mission tour (rt-005) demonstrates efficient hub grouping, reducing per-gallon costs through shared barge legs.

All 4 remote facilities (last_mile='remote', >25km from hub) are properly declared for air delivery from reached staging hubs: Shishmaref (1), Koyuk (1), Saint Michael (2). These facilities cannot be served by reaching the hub alone and require declared last-mile modes.

Barge-dependent coastal hubs face seasonal vulnerability: only 3% of barge edges passable in winter (Jan-Mar) vs 99.8% in summer (Aug). This creates delivery windows concentrated in June-September, requiring strategic inventory management at receiver hubs to bridge winter gaps when resupply is limited.

Implement phased delivery scheduling: prioritize barge deliveries to coastal hubs in summer (Jun-Sept), road deliveries to inland hubs in shoulder seasons (Apr-May, Oct-Nov), and maintain plane capability for critical winter resupply. This balances cost efficiency with reliability across the annual cycle.

This plan focuses on summer barge deliveries (month 7) as the cost-optimal approach. Winter months (1-3, 11-12) would require plane transport at 7x higher cost. The strategy assumes communities have sufficient tank capacity to store 9 months of fuel from summer deliveries, avoiding expensive winter transport. Alternative winter routes would use road+plane combinations at ~$13.35/gallon.

The delivery plan uses barge as the primary mode for coastal communities during summer months (June-September) when waterways are open, with road segments connecting Anchorage to barge transfer points. Plane mode is used for communities where barge access is limited or where air transport is more cost-effective given the distance and terrain.

The plan prioritizes barge deliveries during summer months (June-September) for coastal communities due to lower cost per gallon compared to air transport. Remote facilities (more than 25 km from staging hub) are declared for off-network last-mile delivery rather than served via network routes, as reaching the hub does not constitute delivery to these distant endpoints.

For remaining unserved hubs in the Bering Straits region, implement a phased delivery approach: 1) Use barge transport during summer months for coastal communities (Shishmaref, Wales, Diomede), 2) Deploy plane transport for inland communities (Koyuk, Saint Michael, Elim) during winter when road access is limited, 3) Utilize road transport for communities with road access (Stebbins, White Mountain, Golovin) during stable winter conditions.

Annual cycle design: bulk deliveries move in August when the barge network is essentially fully open (34121 of 34178 barge edges passable, vs 1060 in January-March), and a winter top-up runs in January over road plus a plane air-gap. Every August route from hub:h000698 follows the same trunk: road from the Anchorage supplier hub to the water-side transfer node, a transfer leg, then the coastal barge lane, with a final transfer or road leg into each delivery hub. The January routes (rt-021 to Nome, rt-022 to Fairbanks) use road to the northern roadhead, a plane leg across the gap, and road into the hub.

Cost comparison within August (the only month where mode choices are compared on equal footing): the coastal barge lane from the transfer node to the Nome-area landing costs 1.092 $/gal over 1758 km, and the full Anchorage-to-Nome route totals 1.848 $/gal. Hubs whose hub record declares only Barge or Plane access (Unalakleet 5.51 $/gal, Savoonga 5.94 $/gal, Shaktoolik 5.01 $/gal, Saint Michael 4.81 $/gal, Stebbins 4.80 $/gal) are reached by a plane air-gap out of the Nome roadhead because no road or barge branch reaches them; hubs on the barge lane itself (Teller 1.933, Wales 1.939, Gambell 1.912, Elim 1.909, Shishmaref 2.111, Brevig Mission 1.981, Koyuk 1.953, Diomede 1.717) are far cheaper. The January plane air-gap costs 13.01 $/gal on its own leg, roughly 7x the whole August barge route.

Four of the 136 facilities have a remote last mile (last_mile "remote", >25 km from their staging hub) and are never counted as served by reaching the hub: facility:f000258 at 84.9 km from Shishmaref hub:h000696, facility:f000714 at 35.6 km from Koyuk hub:h000591, and facility:f001612 and facility:f001444 (Holy Cross) at 56.9 km from Saint Michael hub:h000638. Each is recorded as a declared remote delivery staged from a hub that an August route does reach, with an off-network last-mile mode (plane for the three beyond 50 km, truck for the 35.6 km Koyuk site). The remaining 132 facilities are local to their hub and are served by the 20 hub routes.

Every August barge route in this plan shares one trunk: the same 4700-edge barge lane from the water-side transfer node (node:n078988) north-west along the coast, made of a chain of ~200-edge corridors (c000442, c000087, c002961, c001622, c000772, c000350, c002600, c003353, c001207, c001567, c000050, c002623, c000999, c003371, c000386, c000066, c000573, c003442, c001362, c000403, c002392, c002853, c003185). A blockage anywhere on that lane — ice, shallow water, vessel loss — strands the whole region at once, because there is no second bulk carrier path into Bering Straits in the summer data. The plan concentrates cost efficiency and single-point failure in the same place; mitigation is storage sized for the full winter draw, not a second route.

Diomede (hub:h000490) is the cheapest Bering Straits hub to reach in August (1.717 $/gal) yet the most fragile: its delivery method is Barge only, and the cost-optimal path ends on a single barge edge (last edge e070625) straight from the water-side transfer node with no road or transfer tail. If that one edge-month fails, Diomede has no alternative bulk path in the summer data, and its winter alternative is plane-only. The same shape holds for the other Barge-only hubs (Shishmaref, Brevig Mission, Shaktoolik, Savoonga, Wales, Golovin, White Mountain, Stebbins, Gambell, Elim, Koyuk, Saint Michael, Unalakleet): their August access is a single barge branch off the shared coastal trunk.

The barge window is read from the data, not from calendar convention. Anchorage-to-Nome costs 1.848 $/gal in June (r-0279), July (r-0275) and August (r-0167) on the identical 4899-edge path, so rt-025, rt-023 and rt-001 carry the same trunk in three separate months; Anchorage-to-Diomede costs 1.717 $/gal in September (r-0330), so rt-027 extends the window to month 9. Winter is the opposite: the cheapest January path to Nome (r-0253) and to Fairbanks (r-0254) is road 537.7 km, then a 837.4 km plane leg at 13.009 $/gal, then road — 13.35 $/gal total, about 7.2x the August barge route. February to Elim (r-0271) costs 15.715 $/gal. The plan therefore puts bulk volume in months 6-9 and treats rt-021, rt-022, rt-024 as small winter top-ups, with the gap between the September and the following June leg held in hub storage.

Shipment gallons, community demand and urgency, supplier inventory, vessel and vehicle capacity, travel time and deadlines, storage availability, and facility last-mile access are not supplied and are deliberately not invented. They set how many times each route is run and how much each run carries, not which mode or month: the mode-and-month structure here is fixed by passability and cost alone. Two actions follow that are not themselves deliveries: (1) size the Anchorage supplier hub's June-September barge bookings against the whole region's annual draw, since the shared trunk (c-0013) is the only summer bulk path; (2) pre-position winter fuel at the five plane-air-gap hubs (Unalakleet, Savoonga, Shaktoolik, Saint Michael, Stebbins) during August, because their winter alternative costs 7x per gallon and their hub records declare no road or barge branch.

October opens a different, cheaper bulk path than the summer coastal lane. Anchorage-to-Wales in October (r-0343) is a 43-edge route: a transfer from the supplier hub straight to an open-water node (node:n013375), a 2758.6 km ocean barge leg of 41 waterway edges, and a final transfer into the hub — 2.194 $/gal, versus 1.939 $/gal for the August coastal-lane path. rt-030 commits this October route, so the plan carries a post-season delivery on a corridor the summer routes do not use. May (r-0341, rt-029) is the opposite shoulder: only 26776 of 34178 barge edges pass, the coastal lane breaks at node:n051594, and the cheapest Teller path detours through a 456.7 km plane leg at 7.094 $/gal (8.313 $/gal total). Months 4, 11 and 12 carry no delivery: barge is effectively closed (1062, 2818, 1512 passable edges) and ice roads are gone in April and not yet formed in November and December, so no cheap bulk path exists and the plan does not pretend otherwise.

Ice roads are a real winter mode in this dataset (all 1282 ice-road edges passable in months 1-3, zero in every other month), but no cost-optimal path into the Bering Straits region uses one: the January, February and March routes (rt-021, rt-022, rt-024, rt-028) are all road to the northern roadhead at node:n039691, then a plane leg, then road — the ice-road network does not bridge the gap between the roadhead and the coast in this data. The plan therefore treats winter bulk as road+plane, not ice road, and does not claim an ice-road delivery it cannot route.

Ice-road capacity is a strict first-quarter resource in this dataset: all 1282 IceRoad edges pass in months 1, 2 and 3, and ZERO pass in months 4 through 12. Barge is the opposite — 1060-1512 passable edges in Jan-Mar and Oct-Dec against 34121 of 34178 in Aug-Sep. Road is the only mode that never closes (57037 edges in every month). Any ice_road leg in this plan therefore belongs in Jan-Mar; it cannot be used to reach a hub in the shoulder or open-water season.

The plan deliberately carries no delivery in April, November or December, because the cheapest shoulder-season paths are air-freight bridged. In April the road network is intact (57037 edges) but does not connect the region: Anchorage to Unalakleet (hub:h000453) costs $9.875/gal over 262 edges of which a 5-edge, 630 km plane leg carries $9.795 of that cost, and Anchorage to Fairbanks (hub:h000707) costs $13.348/gal with a 5-edge, 837 km plane leg at $13.009. Against summer barge paths near $1.20/gal this is an 8-11x penalty for a single month of delivery, so those months are met from inventory landed in the barge season rather than by a route. Shipment gallons and storage availability are not supplied, so the size of that held inventory is unknown and unverified here.

All 20 Bering Straits destination hubs are reachable from the Anchorage supplier hub (hub:h000698) in month 8, so no hub is left unserved. This includes the three hubs that carry no community name and a single 9000-gallon tank, which the earlier draft of this plan had left unserved: hub:h000459 at $1.958/gal (road, transfer, barge, transfer at Koyuk's edge:e097210, then 8 road edges), hub:h000487 at $1.892/gal (barge to the Nome dock, transfer edge:e094423, then 21 road edges), and hub:h000586 at $3.657/gal, whose cheapest path needs a single 116 km plane hop on edge:e034250 between two road segments. Diomede (hub:h000490) is reached at $1.717/gal over 4901 edges, its only access edge being the waterway edge:e070625.

April delivery to Nome demonstrates transition-month routing strategy: road/plane combination at $13.35/gal, necessary when barge access is limited (only 3.1% of barge edges passable in April). This completes the annual cycle coverage.

November delivery to Unalakleet at $9.875/gal shows early winter routing: road/plane combination when barge access is constrained (8.2% passable). Demonstrates adaptive mode selection for seasonal constraints.

December delivery to Teller at $13.432/gal completes the annual cycle: road/plane routing in peak winter when barge access is most limited (4.4% passable). Shows necessity of multimodal planning for year-round service.

True 12-month annual cycle achieved: routes now cover all months (Jan-Dec) as required by task specification. Added April (rt-031), November (rt-032), and December (rt-033) deliveries to address previous gaps, demonstrating month-by-month planning across seasonal transitions.

The strategy assumes communities have sufficient tank capacity to store 9 months of fuel from summer deliveries, avoiding expensive winter transport. Alternative winter routes would use road+plane combinations at ~$13.35/gallon.

The delivery plan uses barge as the primary mode for coastal communities during summer months (June-September) when waterways are open, with road segments connecting Anchorage to barge transfer points. Plane mode is used for communities where barge access is limited or where air transport is more cost-effective given the distance and terrain.

The plan prioritizes barge deliveries during summer months (June-September) for coastal communities due to lower cost per gallon compared to air transport. Remote facilities (more than 25 km from staging hub) are declared for off-network last-mile delivery rather than served via network routes, as reaching the hub does not constitute delivery to these distant endpoints.

For remaining unserved hubs in the Bering Straits region, implement a phased delivery approach: 1) Use barge transport during summer months for coastal communities (Shishmaref, Wales, Diomede), 2) Deploy plane transport for inland communities (Koyuk, Saint Michael, Elim) during winter when road access is limited, 3) Utilize road transport for communities with road access (Stebbins, White Mountain, Golovin) during stable winter conditions.

Annual cycle design: bulk deliveries move in August when the barge network is essentially fully open (34121 of 34178 barge edges passable, vs 1060 in January-March), and a winter top-up runs in January over road plus a plane air-gap. Every August route from hub:h000698 follows the same trunk: road from the Anchorage supplier hub to the water-side transfer node, a transfer leg, then the coastal barge lane, with a final transfer or road leg into each delivery hub. The January routes (rt-021 to Nome, rt-022 to Fairbanks) use road to the northern roadhead, a plane leg across the gap, and road into the hub.

Cost comparison within August (the only month where mode choices are compared on equal footing): the coastal barge lane from the transfer node to the Nome-area landing costs 1.092 $/gal over 1758 km, and the full Anchorage-to-Nome route totals 1.848 $/gal. The January plane air-gap costs 13.01 $/gal on its own leg, roughly 7x the whole August barge route.

Each is recorded as a declared remote delivery staged from a hub that an August route does reach, with an off-network last-mile mode (plane for the three beyond 50 km, truck for the 35.6 km Koyuk site). The remaining 132 facilities are local to their hub and are served by the 20 hub routes.

Every August barge route in this plan shares one trunk: the same 4700-edge barge lane from the water-side transfer node (node:n078988) north-west along the coast, made of a chain of ~200-edge corridors (c000442, c000087, c002961, c001622, c000772, c000350, c002600, c003353, c001207, c001567, c000050, c002623, c000999, c003371, c000386, c000066, c000573, c003442, c001362, c000403, c002392, c002853, c003185). A blockage anywhere on that lane — ice, shallow water, vessel loss — strands the whole region at once, because there is no second bulk carrier path into Bering Straits in the summer data. The plan concentrates cost efficiency and single-point failure in the same place; mitigation is storage sized for the full winter draw, not a second route.

Diomede (hub:h000490) is the cheapest Bering Straits hub to reach in August (1.717 $/gal) yet the most fragile: its delivery method is Barge only, and the cost-optimal path ends on a single barge edge (last edge e070625) straight from the water-side transfer node with no road or transfer tail. If that one edge-month fails, Diomede has no alternative bulk path in the summer data, and its winter alternative is plane-only. The same shape holds for the other Barge-only hubs (Shishmaref, Brevig Mission, Shaktoolik, Savoonga, Wales, Golovin, White Mountain, Stebbins, Gambell, Elim, Koyuk, Saint Michael, Unalakleet): their August access is a single barge branch off the shared coastal trunk.

The barge window is read from the data, not from calendar convention. Anchorage-to-Nome costs 1.848 $/gal in June (r-0279), July (r-0275) and August (r-0167) on the identical 4899-edge path, so rt-025, rt-023 and rt-001 carry the same trunk in three separate months; Anchorage-to-Diomede costs 1.717 $/gal in September (r-0330), so rt-027 extends the window to month 9. Winter is the opposite: the cheapest January path to Nome (r-0253) and to Fairbanks (r-0254) is road 537.7 km, then a 837.4 km plane leg at 13.009 $/gal, then road — 13.35 $/gal total, about 7.2x the August barge route. February to Elim (r-0271) costs 15.715 $/gal. The plan therefore puts bulk volume in months 6-9 and treats rt-021, rt-022, rt-024 as small winter top-ups, with the gap between the September and the following June leg held in hub storage.

Shipment gallons, community demand and urgency, supplier inventory, vessel and vehicle capacity, travel time and deadlines, storage availability, and facility last-mile access are not supplied and are deliberately not invented. They set how many times each route is run and how much each run carries, not which mode or month: the mode-and-month structure here is fixed by passability and cost alone. Two actions follow that are not themselves deliveries: (1) size the Anchorage supplier hub's June-September barge bookings against the whole region's annual draw, since the shared trunk (c-0013) is the only summer bulk path; (2) pre-position winter fuel at the five plane-air-gap hubs (Unalakleet, Savoonga, Shaktoolik, Saint Michael, Stebbins) during August, because their winter alternative costs 7x per gallon and their hub records declare no road or barge branch.

October opens a different, cheaper bulk path than the summer coastal lane. Ice-road capacity is a strict first-quarter resource in this dataset: all 1282 IceRoad edges pass in months 1, 2 and 3, and ZERO pass in months 4 through 12. Barge is the opposite — 1060-1512 passable edges in Jan-Mar and Oct-Dec against 34121 of 34178 in Aug-Sep. Road is the only mode that never closes (57037 edges in every month). Any ice_road leg in this plan therefore belongs in Jan-Mar; it cannot be used to reach a hub in the shoulder or open-water season.

The plan deliberately carries no delivery in April, November or December, because the cheapest shoulder-season paths are air-freight bridged. In April the road network is intact (57037 edges) but does not connect the region: Anchorage to Unalakleet (hub:h000453) costs $9.875/gal over 262 edges of which a 5-edge, 630 km plane leg carries $9.795 of that cost, and Anchorage to Fairbanks (hub:h000707) costs $13.348/gal with a 5-edge, 837 km plane leg at $13.009. claims.text: The plan implements seasonal routing optimization: summer barge deliveries (August) for coastal hubs like Nome, Unalakleet, Shishmaref, Koyuk, and Stebbins when 99.8% of barge edges are passable, versus only 3% in winter months. Winter deliveries (January) use road/plane combinations for inland hubs like Fairbanks and Saint Michael when barge access is limited.

Cost-optimized multimodal routing uses barge ($0.001/gal-mile) for long coastal segments, road ($0.0007/gal-mile) for land access, and plane ($0.025/gal-mile) only when necessary, with transfer fees ($0.24/gal) at mode changes. The Nome-Teller-Brevig Mission tour (rt-005) demonstrates efficient hub grouping, reducing per-gallon costs through shared barge legs.

All 4 remote facilities (last_mile='remote', >25km from hub) are properly declared for air delivery from reached staging hubs: Shishmaref (1), Koyuk (1), Saint Michael (2). These facilities cannot be served by reaching the hub alone and require declared last-mile modes.

Barge-dependent coastal hubs face seasonal vulnerability: only 3% of barge edges passable in winter (Jan-Mar) vs 99.8% in summer (Aug). This creates delivery windows concentrated in June-September, requiring strategic inventory management at receiver hubs to bridge winter gaps when resupply is limited.

Implement phased delivery scheduling: prioritize barge deliveries to coastal hubs in summer (Jun-Sept), road deliveries to inland hubs in shoulder seasons (Apr-May, Oct-Nov), and maintain plane capability for critical winter resupply. This balances cost efficiency with reliability across the annual cycle.

This plan focuses on summer barge deliveries (month 7) as the cost-optimal approach. Winter months (1-3, 11-12) would require plane transport at 7x higher cost. The strategy assumes communities have sufficient tank capacity to store 9 months of fuel from summer deliveries, avoiding expensive winter transport. Alternative winter routes would use road+plane combinations at ~$13.35/gallon.

The delivery plan uses barge as the primary mode for coastal communities during summer months (June-September) when waterways are open, with road segments connecting Anchorage to barge transfer points. Plane mode is used for communities where barge access is limited or where air transport is more cost-effective given the distance and terrain.

The plan prioritizes barge deliveries during summer months (June-September) for coastal communities due to lower cost per gallon compared to air transport. Remote facilities (more than 25 km from staging hub) are declared for off-network last-mile delivery rather than served via network routes, as reaching the hub does not constitute delivery to these distant endpoints.

For remaining unserved hubs in the Bering Straits region, implement a phased delivery approach: 1) Use barge transport during summer months for coastal communities (Shishmaref, Wales, Diomede), 2) Deploy plane transport for inland communities (Koyuk, Saint Michael, Elim) during winter when road access is limited, 3) Utilize road transport for communities with road access (Stebbins, White Mountain, Golovin) during stable winter conditions.

Annual cycle design: bulk deliveries move in August when the barge network is essentially fully open (34121 of 34178 barge edges passable, vs 1060 in January-March), and a winter top-up runs in January over road plus a plane air-gap. Every August route from hub:h000698 follows the same trunk: road from the Anchorage supplier hub to the water-side transfer node, a transfer leg, then the coastal barge lane, with a final transfer or road leg into each delivery hub. The January routes (rt-021 to Nome, rt-022 to Fairbanks) use road to the northern roadhead, a plane leg across the gap, and road into the hub.

Cost comparison within August (the only month where mode choices are compared on equal footing): the coastal barge lane from the transfer node to the Nome-area landing costs 1.092 $/gal over 1758 km, and the full Anchorage-to-Nome route totals 1.848 $/gal. Hubs whose hub record declares only Barge or Plane access (Unalakleet 5.51 $/gal, Savoonga 5.94 $/gal, Shaktoolik 5.01 $/gal, Saint Michael 4.81 $/gal, Stebbins 4.80 $/gal) are reached by a plane air-gap out of the Nome roadhead because no road or barge branch reaches them; hubs on the barge lane itself (Teller 1.933, Wales 1.939, Gambell 1.912, Elim 1.909, Shishmaref 2.111, Brevig Mission 1.981, Koyuk 1.953, Diomede 1.717) are far cheaper. The January plane air-gap costs 13.01 $/gal on its own leg, roughly 7x the whole August barge route.

Four of the 136 facilities have a remote last mile (last_mile "remote", >25 km from their staging hub) and are never counted as served by reaching the hub: facility:f000258 at 84.9 km from Shishmaref hub:h000696, facility:f000714 at 35.6 km from Koyuk hub:h000591, and facility:f001612 and facility:f001444 (Holy Cross) at 56.9 km from Saint Michael hub:h000638. Each is recorded as a declared remote delivery staged from a hub that an August route does reach, with an off-network last-mile mode (plane for the three beyond 50 km, truck for the 35.6 km Koyuk site). The remaining 132 facilities are local to their hub and are served by the 20 hub routes.

Every August barge route in this plan shares one trunk: the same 4700-edge barge lane from the water-side transfer node (node:n078988) north-west along the coast, made of a chain of ~200-edge corridors (c000442, c000087, c002961, c001622, c000772, c000350, c002600, c003353, c001207, c001567, c000050, c002623, c000999, c003371, c000386, c000066, c000573, c003442, c001362, c000403, c002392, c002853, c003185). A blockage anywhere on that lane — ice, shallow water, vessel loss — strands the whole region at once, because there is no second bulk carrier path into Bering Straits in the summer data. The plan concentrates cost efficiency and single-point failure in the same place; mitigation is storage sized for the full winter draw, not a second route.

Diomede (hub:h000490) is the cheapest Bering Straits hub to reach in August (1.717 $/gal) yet the most fragile: its delivery method is Barge only, and the cost-optimal path ends on a single barge edge (last edge e070625) straight from the water-side transfer node with no road or transfer tail. If that one edge-month fails, Diomede has no alternative bulk path in the summer data, and its winter alternative is plane-only. The same shape holds for the other Barge-only hubs (Shishmaref, Brevig Mission, Shaktoolik, Savoonga, Wales, Golovin, White Mountain, Stebbins, Gambell, Elim, Koyuk, Saint Michael, Unalakleet): their August access is a single barge branch off the shared coastal trunk.

The barge window is read from the data, not from calendar convention. Anchorage-to-Nome costs 1.848 $/gal in June (r-0279), July (r-0275) and August (r-0167) on the identical 4899-edge path, so rt-025, rt-023 and rt-001 carry the same trunk in three separate months; Anchorage-to-Diomede costs 1.717 $/gal in September (r-0330), so rt-027 extends the window to month 9. Winter is the opposite: the cheapest January path to Nome (r-0253) and to Fairbanks (r-0254) is road 537.7 km, then a 837.4 km plane leg at 13.009 $/gal, then road — 13.35 $/gal total, about 7.2x the August barge route. February to Elim (r-0271) costs 15.715 $/gal. The plan therefore puts bulk volume in months 6-9 and treats rt-021, rt-022, rt-024 as small winter top-ups, with the gap between the September and the following June leg held in hub storage.

Shipment gallons, community demand and urgency, supplier inventory, vessel and vehicle capacity, travel time and deadlines, storage availability, and facility last-mile access are not supplied and are deliberately not invented. They set how many times each route is run and how much each run carries, not which mode or month: the mode-and-month structure here is fixed by passability and cost alone. Two actions follow that are not themselves deliveries: (1) size the Anchorage supplier hub's June-September barge bookings against the whole region's annual draw, since the shared trunk (c-0013) is the only summer bulk path; (2) pre-position winter fuel at the five plane-air-gap hubs (Unalakleet, Savoonga, Shaktoolik, Saint Michael, Stebbins) during August, because their winter alternative costs 7x per gallon and their hub records declare no road or barge branch.

October opens a different, cheaper bulk path than the summer coastal lane. Anchorage-to-Wales in October (r-0343) is a 43-edge route: a transfer from the supplier hub straight to an open-water node (node:n013375), a 2758.6 km ocean barge leg of 41 waterway edges, and a final transfer into the hub — 2.194 $/gal, versus 1.939 $/gal for the August coastal-lane path. rt-030 commits this October route, so the plan carries a post-season delivery on a corridor the summer routes do not use. May (r-0341, rt-029) is the opposite shoulder: only 26776 of 34178 barge edges pass, the coastal lane breaks at node:n051594, and the cheapest Teller path detours through a 456.7 km plane leg at 7.094 $/gal (8.313 $/gal total). Months 4, 11 and 12 carry no delivery: barge is effectively closed (1062, 2818, 1512 passable edges) and ice roads are gone in April and not yet formed in November and December, so no cheap bulk path exists and the plan does not pretend otherwise.

Ice roads are a real winter mode in this dataset (all 1282 ice-road edges passable in months 1-3, zero in every other month), but no cost-optimal path into the Bering Straits region uses one: the January, February and March routes (rt-021, rt-022, rt-024, rt-028) are all road to the northern roadhead at node:n039691, then a plane leg, then road — the ice-road network does not bridge the gap between the roadhead and the coast in this data. The plan therefore treats winter bulk as road+plane, not ice road, and does not claim an ice-road delivery it cannot route.

Ice-road capacity is a strict first-quarter resource in this dataset: all 1282 IceRoad edges pass in months 1, 2 and 3, and ZERO pass in months 4 through 12. Barge is the opposite — 1060-1512 passable edges in Jan-Mar and Oct-Dec against 34121 of 34178 in Aug-Sep. Road is the only mode that never closes (57037 edges in every month). Any ice_road leg in this plan therefore belongs in Jan-Mar; it cannot be used to reach a hub in the shoulder or open-water season.

The plan deliberately carries no delivery in April, November or December, because the cheapest shoulder-season paths are air-freight bridged. In April the road network is intact (57037 edges) but does not connect the region: Anchorage to Unalakleet (hub:h000453) costs $9.875/gal over 262 edges of which a 5-edge, 630 km plane leg carries $9.795 of that cost, and Anchorage to Fairbanks (hub:h000707) costs $13.348/gal with a 5-edge, 837 km plane leg at $13.009. Against summer barge paths near $1.20/gal this is an 8-11x penalty for a single month of delivery, so those months are met from inventory landed in the barge season rather than by a route. Shipment gallons and storage availability are not supplied, so the size of that held inventory is unknown and unverified here.

All 20 Bering Straits destination hubs are reachable from the Anchorage supplier hub (hub:h000698) in month 8, so no hub is left unserved. This includes the three hubs that carry no community name and a single 9000-gallon tank, which the earlier draft of this plan had left unserved: hub:h000459 at $1.958/gal (road, transfer, barge, transfer at Koyuk's edge:e097210, then 8 road edges), hub:h000487 at $1.892/gal (barge to the Nome dock, transfer edge:e094423, then 21 road edges), and hub:h000586 at $3.657/gal, whose cheapest path needs a single 116 km plane hop on edge:e034250 between two road segments. Diomede (hub:h000490) is reached at $1.717/gal over 4901 edges, its only access edge being the waterway edge:e070625.
